claims.text: A nanoscale aluminide coating can be deposited on zirconium-alloy nuclear-fuel cladding by physical vapor deposition.
The aluminide coating converts into a continuous Al2O3 scale during high-temperature oxidation.
The resulting Al2O3 scale adheres to the coated zirconium-alloy cladding.
Aluminum in the coating oxidizes preferentially to form Al2O3.
The Al2O3 scale is stable and has low oxygen permeability under the stated high-temperature conditions.
The Al2O3 scale impedes oxygen diffusion to the underlying zirconium alloy.
Impeded oxygen diffusion slows oxidation of the underlying zirconium alloy.
Aluminide-coated cladding will have a lower oxidation-induced weight gain than uncoated cladding under identical high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
Aluminide-coated cladding will develop a thinner oxide scale than uncoated cladding under identical high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
The nanoscale aluminide coating will preserve the mechanical performance of zirconium-alloy cladding in service.
The nanoscale aluminide coating will preserve the thermal performance of zirconium-alloy cladding in service.
Uncoated zirconium-alloy cladding typically develops a porous ZrO2 scale during high-temperature oxidation.
The high-temperature ZrO2 scale on uncoated cladding is less protective than the proposed Al2O3 scale.
The beneficial effect requires the coating to remain sufficiently thin and well adhered.
A coating that is insufficiently thin or poorly adhered may adversely affect heat transfer, mechanical strength, or overall service performance.
Exposure to steam at approximately 1200°C is representative of a severe-accident oxidation condition for zirconium-alloy cladding.
